blocks.label: Code Generation with Claude Code
blocks.narrative: A six-person team uses Claude Code to build and refactor a payments-adjacent service. The repository holds application code, a large test suite, infrastructure definitions and a set of house conventions the team has written down. The questions below follow their first quarter of working this way.

blocks.label: Developer Productivity with Claude
blocks.narrative: The same team extends Claude Code beyond editing: an issue tracker and a design-system server are connected over MCP, and a coordinator agent fans work out to specialists for large investigations. The questions below follow that setup as it is put under load.

blocks.label: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
blocks.narrative: The same repository runs Claude Code as an automated reviewer in its pipeline, and separately as a nightly analysis job. The team is midway through hardening both. The questions below follow that work.

blocks.label: Structured Data Extraction
blocks.narrative: A second pipeline extracts structured records from insurance claim packs — a claim form, an adjuster's narrative, repair quotes and correspondence, arriving together as one multi-page bundle. Records feed a claims system, and a small team reviews a portion before payment is authorised. The questions below follow this pipeline as it is tuned.

questions.stem: Two engineers have Claude Code applying the house conventions correctly. A third joins, clones the same repository on the same branch, and gets none of them — no naming rules, no error-handling standard. All three run the same version and the same commands. The conventions live in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the two machines where they work. What is the fix?
options: Have the new engineer run `/memory` after cloning, which loads the configuration hierarchy for the session.
Have the two working engineers export their configuration and send it to the new engineer to place in the same path.
Move the conventions into the repository at `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, where they are version-controlled and arrive with every clone.
Add the conventions to the repository README, which every engineer reads and which Claude Code picks up from the project root.

whyRight.text: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user scope — personal to a machine, outside the repository and never version-controlled. Two engineers happen to have it because they each wrote it; a clone carries nothing from either. Conventions the whole team should get on clone belong in the project scope inside the repository, which is what makes them arrive with the code.

whyWrong.text: `/memory` reports which configuration files are currently loaded. It is a diagnostic, not a loader, and it cannot surface a file that does not exist on the new engineer's machine.
Copying the file by hand gets the third engineer working and leaves the fourth in the same position. It also creates three copies that drift independently, with no mechanism to keep them in step.
The README is documentation for humans and is not part of the configuration hierarchy. Placing conventions there means they are version-controlled and still never loaded into context.

questions.stem: A refactoring session runs long. Constraints stated early — that one module must keep its public signature, and that a particular helper is deprecated — are honoured at first and then quietly violated around turn twenty, even though nothing removed them from the conversation. What is the effective mitigation?
options: Raise the model's temperature so it explores less conventional solutions that respect the stated constraints.
Add an instruction telling the model to pay equal attention to all parts of the conversation before acting.
Restate the constraints near the start of each request and put them under explicit section headers so their position is stable rather than buried mid-history.
Move to a model with a larger context window so the early turns are never at risk of falling out of scope.

whyRight.text: Content in the middle of a long input receives less reliable attention than content at its edges — the constraints were not lost, they were positioned badly. The corpus's mitigation is structural: move what must be honoured to a stable, prominent position and mark it with explicit headers, rather than hoping the model weights a buried paragraph correctly.

whyWrong.text: Temperature governs sampling variety, not which parts of a long context are weighted. Raising it makes the violated constraints violated more creatively.

Position effects are not something an instruction overrides. Telling the model to attend evenly is a prompt-based answer to a structural property, and the corpus specifically calls it unreliable for this failure.
Nothing has fallen out of the window — the constraints are still present and still being read. A larger window gives the middle more room to be a middle, which is where the problem lives.

questions.stem: An engineer adds `.claude/rules/schema.md` and reports that running `/memory` afterwards 'did not activate it'. The rule's conventions are still not being applied when they edit a schema file, and they ask whether the command needs a flag to force a reload. What should they be told?
options: `/memory` needs the file path passed as an argument to register a file added after the session started.
`/memory` reports which configuration files are loaded; files load automatically from their position in the hierarchy, so the question is whether the file is in a path that loads at all.
`/memory` only reads user-scope files, so a project-scope file has to be registered through project settings instead.
`/memory` loads configuration once per session, so the session must be restarted with the flag that clears the configuration cache.

whyRight.text: `/memory` is a diagnostic that shows what is currently loaded. It activates nothing, so 'running it did not activate the file' describes the command working as designed. The useful next step is to read its output and check whether the new file sits in a location that loads — which is exactly what the diagnostic is for.

whyWrong.text: This invents an argument for a command that takes none and keeps the engineer's mistaken model — that `/memory` is a loader — intact. They would go looking for a flag that does not exist.
The diagnostic reports across the hierarchy, user and project scope alike. Restricting it to user scope would make it useless for the most common question people ask it.
This treats the symptom as a caching problem and invents a flag to clear it. It also accepts the premise that `/memory` performs loading, which is the misconception to correct.

questions.stem: After an expensive codebase analysis, the team wants to evaluate two migration strategies — one incremental, one big-bang — and compare them fairly. Both should start from the analysis already completed, and neither evaluation should be coloured by the other. What is the correct mechanism?
options: Fork the session at the point the analysis completed, so each strategy is explored in an independent branch from the same baseline.
Continue in one session, evaluating the incremental strategy first and the big-bang strategy afterwards.
Start two fresh sessions and re-run the codebase analysis in each so both evaluations rest on their own reading.
Resume the analysis session twice in sequence, discarding the first evaluation's turns before starting the second.

whyRight.text: Forking is built for exactly this: two branches inherit the context up to the branch point and then diverge independently. The expensive analysis is done once and shared, and neither branch can see the other's reasoning — which is what makes the comparison fair.

whyWrong.text: Sequential evaluation in one session lets the first strategy's reasoning and conclusions shape the second. The comparison is then between a fresh assessment and one made in the shadow of the other.
Two fresh sessions give independence and pay for the expensive analysis twice, and the two readings may differ, so the strategies would be compared against subtly different baselines.
Resuming and discarding turns is an attempt to hand-roll forking. It relies on removing the first evaluation cleanly, which is precisely what a fork does by construction and manual pruning does not.

questions.stem: An engineer is four hours into a session that has explored a large part of the codebase. Responses are becoming vaguer and occasionally reference files that were renamed earlier in the session. They intend to keep working for another two hours. Select TWO steps that fit.
options: Write the accumulated findings to a scratchpad file before doing anything else, so they survive whatever comes next.
Compact the conversation now rather than waiting until the context limit is actually reached.
Restart the session immediately and rebuild understanding by re-exploring the same files.
Continue working and rely on the model to disregard the stale references now that the renames have happened.

whyRight.text: Both correct steps treat context quality as something to manage before it fails. Persisting findings to a scratchpad makes the accumulated knowledge independent of the session, so any later restart is cheap. Compacting proactively during a long session — rather than as an emergency at the limit — is what keeps the remaining two hours working from a clean summary instead of a degraded transcript.

whyWrong.text: Restarting without first persisting anything throws away four hours of accumulated understanding, and re-exploring the same files pays the whole cost again. If a restart is needed, state is saved first and injected into the new session.

The stale tool results are still in the conversation and still available to reason from. Expecting the model to route around content that is present and contradictory is the assumption the observed symptom already disproves.

questions.stem: An engineer wants a `/scaffold` command available to the team. They create `.claude/skills/scaffold.md` in the repository, commit it, and pull on a second machine. The command appears in neither place, and `/memory` lists no skill by that name. The file's contents are correct and its frontmatter parses. What is wrong?
options: The file is correct but skills are user-scope only, so it has to move to `~/.claude/skills/scaffold.md`.
The file needs a `paths` entry in its frontmatter before the command becomes available.
Skills must be declared in the project `CLAUDE.md` before Claude Code will register them.
A skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md` entrypoint, so this must be `.claude/skills/scaffold/SKILL.md` — a loose Markdown file dropped into `.claude/skills/` is not picked up.

whyRight.text: The two locations take different file structures. A command can be a flat Markdown file, but it belongs under `.claude/commands/`. A skill is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` entrypoint, which is what lets it carry supporting files and frontmatter. A bare `.md` sitting directly in `.claude/skills/` matches neither shape and is simply not picked up.

whyWrong.text: Project-scoped skills are supported and are the right choice for something the team should get on clone. Moving it to user scope would make it personal to one machine, which is the opposite of the intent.
`paths` scopes when something applies; it does not make an unrecognised file recognised. Adding frontmatter to a file in the wrong shape leaves it in the wrong shape.
There is no registration step in CLAUDE.md. Skills and commands are discovered from their directories, which is why the directory layout is the thing that matters here.

questions.stem: Before renaming a configuration key, an engineer asks Claude Code to locate every place the string `retry_budget` is read. Claude runs a Glob search for `**/*retry_budget*` and reports two files, both of which merely have the key in their filename. The key is read in eleven places. Which tool should have been used, and why?
options: Grep, because the reads are text inside files and Grep searches file contents, whereas Glob matches file `paths`.
`Glob` with a recursive pattern anchored at the repository root, since the current pattern did not descend into nested directories.
Read on each candidate directory, since neither search tool reliably covers configuration keys.
`Glob` first to narrow the candidate set, then Glob again with the key as a suffix pattern to catch the remaining files.

whyRight.text: The distinction is path versus content. Glob matches file paths against a naming pattern, which is why it returned the two files named after the key and nothing else. Reads of a key are text inside files, and searching text inside files is what Grep does. The eleven call sites were never candidates for a path-matching search.

whyWrong.text: The pattern already descends — that is what the leading `**/` does. However deep it reaches, it is still comparing paths, so it cannot find a key read inside a file whose name does not contain it.
Reading directories one by one to find eleven occurrences loads large amounts of irrelevant content and is the context-budget failure the corpus warns against. Grep answers the question directly.
Two Glob passes are two path searches. No sequence of path patterns finds a string inside a file whose name does not contain it.

questions.stem: A prompt classifies each pull request as a refactor, a feature or a fix, and the label drives which review checklist runs. It carries six examples covering the clear cases. Those are handled well; changes that add a feature while restructuring the code around it are labelled inconsistently, sometimes one way and sometimes the other on near-identical diffs. What would most improve it?
options: Remove the examples and replace them with a longer prose definition of each category.
Add six more examples of clear cases, so the three categories are more thoroughly demonstrated.
Replace the six examples with examples of the genuinely ambiguous mixed cases, each stating the reasoning for the label it received.
Add a fourth category called mixed, so ambiguous changes have somewhere to go.

whyRight.text: Examples earn their place where the decision is hard, and the clear cases are already handled. Targeting the ambiguous mixed changes puts the demonstration where the failure is. Including the reasoning for each label matters as much as the label: it teaches the decision principle rather than the specific case, so the model generalises to mixed changes the examples never showed.

whyWrong.text: This trades demonstration for description in a task where the hard cases resist definition. Prose about category boundaries is exactly what leaves a mixed change to interpretation.
More examples of cases that already work add tokens and teach nothing new. The corpus is specific that example selection should target the ambiguous region rather than reinforce the obvious one.

A mixed bucket relocates the ambiguity rather than resolving it — the model must now decide when a change is mixed enough, which is the same judgement under a new name, and downstream consumers lose the classification they needed.

questions.stem: A long refactoring conversation is approaching the context limit. An engineer proposes dropping the oldest third of the turns from every subsequent request to make room, arguing that the recent turns carry the current state anyway. Those early turns are where the module boundary and the deprecation list were agreed. What is wrong with this, and what should be done instead?
options: Nothing is wrong; dropping the oldest turns is the standard way to bound a conversation, and the model reconstructs what it needs from the remaining ones.
Dropping turns is fine provided the turns removed contain no tool results, since only tool results carry state the model cannot reconstruct.
The oldest turns should be moved into the system prompt instead, which keeps them available without counting towards the conversation length.

The API is stateless and each request carries the whole conversation, so removing turns removes information permanently; summarise the dropped range and keep a verbatim block of the facts that must not degrade.

whyRight.text: Every request sends the full conversation, so a turn that is not sent simply does not exist for that request — there is no server-side memory to fall back on. Cutting the oldest third takes the decisions and constraints agreed there with it. Summarising the dropped range carries the conclusions forward, and holding the exact identifiers and values in a verbatim facts block protects the content summarisation degrades worst.

whyWrong.text: This assumes the model can reconstruct removed content from what remains. It cannot: a constraint agreed in turn four and never restated is unavailable once turn four stops being sent.
Prose turns carry decisions, constraints and agreed approaches that are just as unrecoverable as tool results. The distinction drawn here does not track what is safe to discard.

The system prompt is re-sent with every request and counts towards the same budget, so this relocates content without saving anything. It also fills a slot meant for persistent behavioural constraints with conversation history.

questions.stem: A test fails with a stack trace pointing at one function in one file. The cause is visible in the trace, the fix is a two-line change, and no other module is involved. An engineer asks whether to use plan mode. What is the right answer?
options: Yes — plan mode should be the default for any change to code covered by tests, so the change is reviewed before it is applied.
No — the problem, its location and the fix are all already known, which is the case direct execution is for.
Yes — planning costs little and the plan serves as documentation of why the change was made.
No — plan mode cannot be used for changes driven by a failing test, since it does not run the test suite.

whyRight.text: Plan mode earns its overhead when the approach is genuinely open — multiple files, competing designs, decisions that are expensive to reverse. Here the stack trace has already identified the location and the fix is two lines in one function, so there is nothing left to decide. Direct execution is the textbook fit.

whyWrong.text: Selecting plan mode by whether the code has tests uses the wrong criterion. The decision turns on how much about the change is still undetermined, and here nothing is.
The cost is small but it is paid on every trivial fix, and a plan for a two-line change documents a decision nobody had to make. Commit messages already carry that record.
The conclusion is right and the reason is invented. Nothing prevents plan mode being used on test-driven work; it is simply unnecessary when the problem and fix are both already known.

questions.stem: Yesterday a session analysed a 50-file module and produced a working understanding of its call graph and its test coverage. Overnight three of those files were refactored; the other 47 are untouched. The engineer wants to carry on this morning from where they left off rather than rebuild that understanding. What is the correct approach?
options: Fork the previous session, so the stale analysis is left behind in the original branch.
Resume the named session and continue, since the model will re-read anything it needs as the work proceeds.
Start a fresh session and re-analyse all fifty files, so nothing in context is stale.
Resume the named session and tell it explicitly which three files changed, so it re-analyses just those.

whyRight.text: Most of yesterday's context is still accurate — 47 of 50 files are untouched — so discarding it is waste. Resuming keeps that value, and naming the three changed files gives the agent a targeted re-analysis instead of leaving it to reason from stale tool results. The corpus's worked pattern for this exact situation is resume plus an explicit statement of what changed.

whyWrong.text: A fork inherits the context up to the branch point, so the stale results for the three files come with it. Forking is for exploring divergent approaches from a shared baseline, not for shedding outdated data.

Resuming without saying what changed leaves yesterday's tool results in history as though they were current. The agent has no reason to suspect three of them and may reason confidently from outdated file contents.

Re-analysing all fifty files to account for three that changed discards a large, still-valid body of work. Starting fresh is the right call when prior context is broadly stale, which is not the case here.

questions.stem: A generation step returns a structured change plan through a tool call, and every field in its schema is currently marked required. Reviewers find `rollback_step` and `owning_team` populated with confident-looking values on plans where the request mentioned neither, and the values are plausible enough that two of them were acted on. Select TWO changes that reduce this.
options: Make fields that may legitimately have no value nullable, so the model can report absence instead of supplying something.
State explicit criteria for when each field applies, rather than asking the model to fill the plan sensibly.
Mark every field required, so the model treats the schema as a complete specification and reads the request more carefully.
Raise the model tier for this step, since fabrication is a capability problem that stronger models exhibit less.

whyRight.text: Fabrication here has two sources and each correct option removes one. A required field is an instruction to produce a value, so the model supplies a plausible one when the request is silent — making genuinely optional fields nullable lets it answer honestly. And 'fill the plan sensibly' gives no rule for when a field applies, so explicit criteria replace a judgement call with a decision the model can actually follow.

whyWrong.text: This increases the pressure that produces the behaviour. A required field must be populated, so marking every field required guarantees a value for details the request never mentioned.
Fabrication under a required-field schema is a response to the constraint, not a shortfall in capability. A stronger model asked to produce a value where none exists still produces one.

questions.stem: An agent must change one of six occurrences of `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` in a settings module. Its first Edit attempt reports a non-unique match. It immediately reads the whole 900-line file and writes it back with the single change applied. What should it have done, and why does it matter?
options: Read the file first in every case, since Edit is unreliable on files with repeated identifiers.
Split the settings module so each occurrence sits in its own file, removing the ambiguity permanently.
Widen the match with surrounding context until one occurrence is pinned down, because that stays within Edit and costs a fraction of the context that reading 900 lines consumes.
Use replace-all, since a non-unique match means the identifier is used consistently and all six should change together.

whyRight.text: A non-unique match is an ordinary condition with a documented recovery: add surrounding context to the anchor until it identifies one occurrence. Edit touches only the matched text, while Read plus Write pulls 900 lines into context and rewrites all of them to change one. Escalating on the first obstacle spends a large amount of context to avoid a small amount of precision.

whyWrong.text: This makes the fallback the default. Edit handles repeated identifiers perfectly well once the anchor is specific enough, and reading every file before editing it is the context-budget failure the corpus warns against.
Restructuring source files so a text search becomes easier is a large, unrelated change driven by a tool message. It also does not help with the next file that repeats an identifier.
Replace-all is the right recovery when every occurrence genuinely should change, and the premise here is that exactly one should. Applying it would silently change five values nobody asked to touch.

questions.stem: An engineer delegates a broad 'find everywhere the pricing rules are applied' investigation to a subagent. A colleague argues this is pointless because only one investigation is running, so there is nothing to parallelise. What is the stronger argument for delegating?
options: Subagents run on a cheaper model tier by default, so broad searches cost less when delegated.
Context isolation — the subagent absorbs the verbose search and file output, and only its conclusion returns to the main conversation.
Subagents have access to search tools the main session does not, so the investigation is more thorough.
Delegation checkpoints the main session, so the investigation can be retried without losing the main conversation.

whyRight.text: Parallelism is one benefit of subagents and not the main one here. A broad investigation generates a large volume of intermediate output, and running it in an isolated context keeps all of that out of the main conversation — the main session receives the finding rather than the search. That is worth doing with a single investigation and no concurrency at all.

whyWrong.text: Model tier is configurable per subagent and is not what makes delegation the right call. The argument would also collapse the moment the subagent ran on the same tier.
A subagent's tools are a subset chosen for it, not a superset unavailable to the main session. Delegation does not unlock capability that was otherwise out of reach.

This describes a benefit of session management rather than of delegation, and it is not the mechanism at work. The main conversation is protected here because the verbose output never enters it, not because it can be rolled back.

questions.stem: Three MCP tools return timestamps in three formats — Unix epoch, ISO 8601 and a locale string. The agent reasons over all three and makes date-comparison errors a few times a week. A developer proposes adding a system-prompt paragraph explaining each tool's format and asking the model to convert before comparing. What is the better approach?
options: A `PostToolUse` hook that normalises each tool's timestamps to one format before the result reaches the model.
A `PreToolUse` hook that rejects calls to tools whose timestamp format has not been declared.
Few-shot examples showing each of the three formats converted correctly, so the model learns the conversions.
A wrapper tool that calls all three and returns a merged result, so the model only ever sees one tool's output.

whyRight.text: Data normalisation after a tool runs is precisely what PostToolUse hooks are for. Converting the three formats in the hook means the model always receives one consistent representation, deterministically, regardless of which tool produced it — where a prompt explanation leaves the conversion to the model's judgement on every call and produces the errors already being seen.

whyWrong.text: PreToolUse runs before execution and can block a call. There is nothing here to block — the calls are legitimate and their results merely need reshaping, which happens after they return.

Examples make correct conversion more likely and still leave it to the model on every comparison. The corpus prefers hooks precisely where a consistent transformation is wanted every time rather than usually.

A merging wrapper forces all three tools to be called together whenever any one is needed, and it still has to normalise the formats somewhere. It adds coupling to solve a problem the hook solves in place.

questions.stem: An MCP server exposes `find_issue`, described as 'issue search'. Asked to check whether a bug has already been reported, the agent almost always runs a Grep across the repository instead and reports what it finds in code comments. The MCP server is connected and its tool is available. What is the likely cause?
options: The MCP tool's description is too sparse to compete with the detailed built-in tool descriptions, so the model reaches for the tool it understands better.
MCP tools are ranked below built-in tools when both could apply, so a built-in wins whenever one is plausible.
The server is connected but its tools are not in the agent's allowed set, so the call would fail and is silently skipped.
`Grep` returns faster, and the model prefers lower-latency tools when both can answer the question.

whyRight.text: A model selects the tool whose description best matches the task, and 'issue search' says almost nothing — not what it searches, not what it returns, not when to prefer it. The built-in tools carry detailed descriptions, so they win the comparison. Expanding the MCP description to state its capability and output is what makes it competitive.

whyWrong.text: There is no built-in-first ranking. Selection is driven by how well each description matches the request, which is why improving the description changes the outcome.
A tool outside the allowed set produces a permission outcome, not a silent substitution. The observed behaviour is a choice between two available tools, not a blocked call.
Tool selection is not latency-ranked, and the model has no reliable knowledge of how long a given tool will take. This attributes an optimisation to the model that it is not performing.

questions.stem: A coordinator must answer three questions before a design review: which components use a deprecated token, which tests cover the checkout flow, and what the issue tracker holds against this milestone. None of the three depends on either of the others. The coordinator currently spawns one specialist, waits, spawns the next, and so on. What should change?
options: Collapse the three into one specialist with all the tools, removing two spawn round-trips.
Keep the sequence but have each specialist pass its findings to the next, so later work benefits from earlier context.
Issue all three spawn calls in a single coordinator response so the specialists run concurrently, and assemble the returns when they complete.
Keep the sequence and start with the fastest question, so the coordinator has something to report sooner.

whyRight.text: Independent subtasks should be dispatched together. Several spawn calls in one coordinator response run concurrently, so the wait becomes the slowest question rather than the sum of all three. Nothing here creates an ordering constraint, so the current serialisation is pure latency.

whyWrong.text: One specialist holding every tool processes the three questions one after another inside itself and widens its tool surface, which degrades selection. The round-trips were never the dominant cost.

Chaining manufactures a dependency the task does not have, keeps the total time as the sum of the parts, and lets one specialist's framing colour the next. It also routes information between subagents rather than through the coordinator.
Reordering changes when partial results appear and leaves the total as the sum of the three. It optimises the ordering of a serialisation instead of removing it.

questions.stem: Asked how a checkout total is calculated, the agent reads all 34 files in the checkout package before answering. The answer is correct, the main context is nearly full afterwards, and the follow-up question performs noticeably worse. What is the correct investigation strategy?
options: Read the package's entry point first, then follow imports outward only as far as the question requires.
`Grep` for the calculation's entry point, then Read only the files that trace shows are on the path.
Read all 34 files as before but summarise each one immediately, keeping only the summaries in context.
Delegate the same read-everything approach to a subagent, so the main context is unaffected.

whyRight.text: Incremental investigation is the documented pattern: search to locate the relevant entry points, then read only what the trace requires. It answers the question with a fraction of the content, which is why the follow-up still has room to work in. Loading a whole package before knowing what is relevant is the context-budget failure the corpus names directly.

whyWrong.text: Following imports from an entry point is better than reading everything and still starts from a guess about where to begin. Searching for the calculation locates the entry point rather than assuming it.
The full content still passes through the context to be summarised, so the cost is paid and a lossy summary is what remains. It adds a step without avoiding the load.

Delegation protects the main context and is worth doing for genuinely broad investigations, but it does not make an indiscriminate strategy correct — the subagent now exhausts its own context reading 33 irrelevant files.

questions.stem: A coordinator is asked to prepare a migration plan for a shared authentication module. It splits the work into 'update the login handler', 'update the session handler' and 'update the token refresh handler'. The resulting plan says nothing about the four services that call the module, and the migration breaks two of them. Where is the defect?
options: In the specialists, which should have investigated beyond their assignments once they saw a shared module.
In the assembly step, which should have cross-referenced the three returns to detect the missing consumer analysis.
In the number of specialists, since four callers would need four more assignments to be covered.
In the coordinator's decomposition, which partitioned inside the module and never assigned anyone the consumers of it.

whyRight.text: The three assignments carve up the module's internals, so the four calling services were never anyone's responsibility. Specialists cover what they are given, and no amount of diligence within an assignment reaches outside it. A coverage gap traces back to the point where the task became subtasks.

whyWrong.text: A specialist that wanders outside its assignment produces unpredictable overlap and gaps of a different kind. The corpus locates this failure in the partitioning, not in the discipline of the agents executing it.

Assembly can only reconcile what it receives, and nothing about the calling services was produced by any specialist. A cross-check over three internal analyses cannot surface a fourth topic that was never investigated.
Adding specialists to a decomposition that only names internals hands out more internal slices. Capacity is not what is missing; a dimension of the problem is.

questions.stem: A specialist is being defined to audit dependency licences against the team's approved list. It needs to read manifests and search the repository, must not modify anything, and will be spawned by the coordinator once per release. The approved list and the manifest locations are both known to the coordinator. Select TWO configuration choices that follow the corpus.
options: Give it a read-only tool set — read and search tools only — rather than the full set with an instruction not to write.
State the licence policy and the manifest locations in the prompt the coordinator passes it, since it inherits neither from the coordinator.
Give it the full tool set so it can fix any violation it finds without a second round-trip.
Have it write its findings directly into the issue tracker so the coordinator is not a bottleneck.

whyRight.text: Least privilege and explicit context are the two rules governing subagent definition. A tool a specialist does not hold is a tool it cannot misuse, which is stronger than an instruction not to use one. And a subagent's context starts empty, so the policy and the manifest locations only exist for it if the coordinator writes them into the prompt.

whyWrong.text: Granting write access so an auditor can also remediate turns a read-only role into one that can change the repository, and it does so to save a round-trip. The corpus scopes tools to the role rather than to the convenience.

Writing findings out to an external system routes results around the coordinator, which loses visibility of what the specialist concluded and cannot handle its errors consistently. Returns flow back through the coordinator.

questions.stem: After rewriting the design-system server's tool descriptions to be precise and distinct, `get_component_spec` is still bypassed roughly a third of the time in favour of a repository search. The system prompt contains the line: 'When asked about components, search the codebase for the component definition.' What does this show?
options: Tool descriptions only influence selection when no system-prompt guidance applies, so descriptions should be removed once the prompt is specific.
A keyword-sensitive system-prompt instruction can override well-written tool descriptions, so the prompt has to be reviewed alongside them.
The rewrite did not take effect, since description changes require the MCP server to be reconnected.
A third of the requests are genuinely about definitions rather than specifications, so the split is the correct behaviour.

whyRight.text: The system prompt and the tool descriptions are read together, and an instruction that names a behaviour by keyword — 'components' plus 'search the codebase' — creates an association strong enough to win against a description that says the same tool should be preferred. Fixing descriptions without reading the prompt leaves a competing instruction in place.

whyWrong.text: This inverts the relationship and would remove the primary lever for tool selection. Descriptions and prompt guidance both matter, which is exactly why a conflict between them produces the observed split.

If the rewrite had not taken effect, the behaviour would be unchanged rather than improved to two-thirds. The partial improvement is evidence the new descriptions are being read and are being outweighed on some requests.

Nothing in the scenario distinguishes the bypassed third by subject matter, and the prompt line names components generally. Declaring the split correct explains away a conflict the prompt visibly creates.

questions.stem: To cut latency, an engineer proposes letting the test-analysis specialist send its findings straight to the code-generation specialist, skipping the coordinator hop and saving roughly four seconds per exchange. Both already run under the same coordinator, and the payload is a short structured summary. What is the objection?
options: Direct exchange between specialists removes the coordinator's visibility of what passed between them, its consistent error handling and its control over what each one receives.
The specialists would need each other's tool definitions, which would widen both tool sets past the reliable range.
Findings sent directly would arrive without the coordinator's formatting, so the receiving specialist could not parse them.
There is no objection provided the coordinator is sent a copy of everything the two specialists exchange.

whyRight.text: Hub-and-spoke routes every exchange through the coordinator, and the reasons are structural rather than stylistic: the coordinator is where failures are handled uniformly, where the flow of information is controlled, and where the run can be observed. A direct channel removes all three, and the corpus rejects it regardless of the efficiency gained.

whyWrong.text: Passing a result does not require holding the other agent's tools. This objects on a mechanism that is not implicated and would evaporate if the two tool sets happened to be small.
Formatting is solvable and is not what the constraint protects. Framing the rule as a serialisation detail invites someone to standardise a payload and proceed.
Copying the coordinator restores a log and not control. It still cannot intervene, cannot handle a failure in the exchange, and cannot decide what the receiving specialist should have been given.

questions.stem: The project `CLAUDE.md` has grown to about 700 lines. Most of it is a set of numbered procedures — how to run a dependency audit, how to prepare a release branch, how to triage a flaky test — each used a few times a month. The rest is genuinely universal. Sessions have become noticeably more expensive. What should be done?
options: Move each procedure into its own skill so it loads when invoked, leaving `CLAUDE.md` holding only the universal standards.
Move the procedures into `.claude/rules/` with globs, so they load only for the relevant file types.
Keep the procedures in `CLAUDE.md` but compress them into shorter summaries to reduce the token cost.
Split `CLAUDE.md` into several files in the same directory, so each session loads only the one it needs.

whyRight.text: CLAUDE.md carries always-loaded universal standards, and a procedure used a few times a month is not that — it is a task workflow. Skills are the on-demand mechanism: the procedure is available when invoked and costs nothing the rest of the time, which is where the 700 lines of per-session expense is going.

whyWrong.text: Path rules load when a matching file is read, which is the wrong trigger for a release-branch or triage procedure. Those are invoked by intent, not by which file is open.
Compression reduces the size of content that should not be resident at all. It also degrades the procedures, which need their steps intact when they are actually run.
Files in the hierarchy are concatenated as they load rather than selected among, so splitting one long file into several in the same directory changes the layout and not the cost.

questions.stem: The issue-tracker server returns `{"isError": true, "message": "Request could not be completed"}` for every failure — an expired token, a rate limit, a malformed query and an unknown project key all produce that string. The agent retries all of them identically and reports the same unhelpful summary to the user. What must the responses carry?
options: A stack trace from the server, so the agent can determine the failure class from the exception type.
The original request echoed back, so the agent can compare what it sent against what the server expected.
A numeric error code the agent can look up against a table supplied in the system prompt.
An error category, an `isRetryable` flag and a description specific enough to name what failed.

whyRight.text: The agent's recovery depends on distinctions the response is not making. A rate limit is worth retrying after a wait, an expired token needs re-authentication, a malformed query needs correcting, and an unknown project key needs escalating. A category, a retryable flag and a specific description are what let the agent tell those apart and take the right path for each.

whyWrong.text: A stack trace exposes server internals and asks the agent to infer semantics from an implementation detail. It is verbose, leaks structure, and still does not state whether a retry would help.
Echoing the request helps only with the malformed-query case and says nothing about the other three. The agent still cannot tell a transient failure from a permanent one.

A code plus a lookup table in the prompt puts the meaning of the error somewhere other than the error, and the table drifts from the server the moment either changes. The response should carry its own semantics.

questions.stem: A release specialist must tag a build before publishing it. Its prompt says so, and about one release in twelve is published untagged. An engineer proposes a classifier in front of the coordinator that identifies release requests and routes them to the release specialist. Why does this not address the problem?
options: A classifier adds a component that itself fails occasionally, so the joint failure rate would be worse than one in twelve.
A classifier would be accurate enough for routing but not for detecting whether a build has been tagged.
A classifier decides which agent handles a request; the failure happens inside the release specialist's own execution sequence, after routing has already succeeded.
Classifiers cannot be placed in front of a coordinator, since the coordinator is the entry point to the system.

whyRight.text: Routing and sequencing are different problems. The requests are already reaching the right specialist — the missing tag happens once it is working, when a prompt-level instruction about ordering is not followed. A classifier improves nothing about the order of operations inside an agent, and the fix belongs in a prerequisite gate that blocks publishing until the tag exists.

whyWrong.text: The compounding-error argument is true of any added component and is beside the point. Even a perfect classifier would leave the one-in-twelve untagged releases exactly where they are.
This grants the classifier a role in checking the tag, which is not what a classifier does. It concedes the wrong framing and then argues about accuracy inside it.
Nothing prevents a routing layer in front of a coordinator. Objecting on architecture avoids the actual reason, which is that routing is not where this failure occurs.

questions.stem: A `delete_branch` tool is occasionally called on branches that still carry unmerged commits — three times last month, twice recoverable from the reflog. The team wants deletion to be impossible unless the agent has first seen exactly what would be removed, and wants that guarantee to hold without depending on the model remembering to check. Which tool design achieves it?
options: One tool with a `dry_run` boolean, defaulting to true, that the agent sets to false on the second call.
Two tools: a preview that returns a short-lived token describing exactly what would be deleted, and a delete that accepts only that token.
One tool with a `confirmed` boolean the agent must set to true, plus a prompt instruction to preview first.
One tool that deletes immediately, paired with a `PostToolUse` hook that restores the branch when open work is detected.

whyRight.text: Binding the destructive call to a token that only the preview can issue makes the preview a precondition of the deletion rather than a habit the model is asked to keep. The token also pins the deletion to the specific state that was previewed, so a branch that changed in between cannot be removed on a stale look.

whyWrong.text: A single tool with a boolean lets the model set it to false on the first call and delete without ever previewing. The default only changes what happens when the parameter is omitted, not what the model is able to do.

A confirmation flag the caller sets itself confirms nothing, and the preview requirement lives in a prompt instruction rather than in the interface. Both halves are probabilistic where a guarantee was asked for.
A PostToolUse hook runs after the deletion, so the branch is already gone when the check fires. Restoration is a recovery path, and it assumes every deletion is reversible.

questions.stem: The team wants Claude to recall architectural decisions made in sessions weeks earlier — why a queue was chosen over polling, which retry library was rejected and on what grounds, and which of two caching strategies was ruled out. Sessions are started fresh each morning and the decisions are currently only in old transcripts. Select TWO approaches that work.
options: Persist each decision with its rationale to a durable store, and retrieve the relevant ones into context when a related question comes up.
Begin a new session by injecting a structured summary of the decisions that bear on the work about to be done.
Keep one long-running session alive indefinitely, re-summarising its history whenever it approaches the context limit.
Move to a model with a larger context window so several weeks of sessions fit without any recall mechanism.

whyRight.text: Recall across sessions has to come from outside the conversation, because the API keeps no state between them. Writing decisions and their rationale to a durable store and retrieving the relevant ones on demand scales without bound, and injecting a structured summary at the start of a session carries the conclusions that matter into the context that needs them.

whyWrong.text: Repeated summarisation of a summary compounds loss at every pass, and the specific content it destroys first — identifiers, the reasons a library was rejected — is exactly what needs to survive. Weeks of decisions cannot be held that way.

A larger window postpones the limit and does not create recall across separate sessions, since each new session starts empty regardless of how large it could grow. It also worsens retrieval, as the relevant decision sits further from the edges of a longer context.

questions.stem: Every file under `infra/` must carry a specific header comment and follow a naming rule, and this must apply automatically whenever Claude edits one of those files — without anyone remembering to ask for it. An engineer proposes writing it as a skill with a `paths` entry. What is the better mechanism, and why?
options: A skill with `paths` is correct, since a paths entry is what makes either mechanism activate on matching files.
A directory-level `CLAUDE.md` inside `infra/`, because directory-scoped configuration is the only mechanism that applies automatically.
A path-scoped rule in `.claude/rules/`, because rules load as background guidance whenever a matching file is read, whereas a skill loads as an invoked workflow.
A pre-commit hook, since conventions that must never be missed cannot be expressed in configuration at all.

whyRight.text: Both mechanisms can be scoped by path, so the discriminator is what each one is. A rule stays in context as background guidance the moment a matching file is read, which is what shapes every edit. A skill is a task-style workflow that loads when it is invoked or matched as an intent. For always-on conventions attached to a file type, rules are the fit.

whyWrong.text: This treats the shared frontmatter field as though it made the two mechanisms equivalent. They are scoped the same way and behave differently once scoped, which is the whole of the distinction.
A directory-level file would work for one directory and is not the only automatic mechanism. It also stops at the directory boundary, so any convention spanning several would need a copy in each.
A commit hook catches violations after they are written and does nothing to guide the edit. It is a useful backstop and not an answer to which configuration mechanism applies the convention.

questions.stem: An audit of 40 modules in one pass produces detailed findings for the first several and thin ones thereafter. An engineer argues that a sharper prompt — explicitly requiring the same six checks on every module — makes a multi-pass architecture unnecessary. What is the flaw in that argument?
options: A sharper prompt would work, but multi-pass is preferred because it is easier to parallelise across workers.
The six checks would need to be listed for each module individually, which makes the prompt too long to be effective.
Prompts are probabilistic, so the six checks would be applied to most modules but not all, leaving a small residual failure rate.

A prompt cannot allocate attention across a long input; the depth falls off because each module competes with 39 others in one pass, which is a property of the architecture rather than of the instruction.

whyRight.text: Requiring six checks does not change how attention is distributed over a 40-module input — the later modules still arrive after everything before them. Multi-pass fixes this structurally by giving each module a pass of its own, so its depth does not depend on its position. A better prompt raises the average and leaves the falloff intact.

whyWrong.text: This concedes the argument and defends multi-pass on operational grounds. Parallelism is a benefit, but the reason multi-pass is required here is that a single pass cannot deliver even depth at all.
Prompt length is not the constraint; the same six checks stated once apply to every module. This objects to a formatting choice rather than to the reasoning.
A uniform small residual rate is not what is observed. The findings degrade with position, which points at attention allocation rather than at ordinary instruction-following variance.

questions.stem: A prompt asks the agent to flag risky dependency upgrades and to attach a confidence score, with anything below 0.7 suppressed. False positives remain high, and inspection shows suppressed items and surfaced items are similar in kind. What should be done first?
options: Calibrate the confidence scores against a labelled set and keep the 0.7 threshold.
Raise the suppression threshold to 0.85, since the current cut-off is admitting too much.
Have the agent produce two independent confidence scores and suppress unless both clear the threshold.
Define explicit criteria for what counts as risky — a major version change, a transitive change to a package on the security list, a maintainer change — and only then consider confidence for routing.

whyRight.text: The scores are being asked to rank judgements against an undefined standard, so similar items land on either side of the cut-off. Confidence is only meaningful once the model knows what it is being confident about — define the categorical criteria first, and confidence routing becomes a useful refinement afterwards rather than a substitute for the definition.

whyWrong.text: Calibration is the right step once there is a stable definition to calibrate against. Labelling a set of items whose criterion nobody has stated reproduces the ambiguity in the labels.

Moving an uncalibrated threshold on an undefined criterion suppresses more of everything. Since the suppressed and surfaced items are already alike, a higher bar loses genuine findings at the same rate as false ones.
Two scores from the same model on the same undefined criterion correlate strongly. It doubles the cost and produces agreement rather than accuracy.

questions.stem: The project `CLAUDE.md` carries three long sections of file-type conventions — Terraform, SQL migrations and React components. Token usage per session has climbed, and engineers editing a React component are paying for the Terraform and SQL sections on every request. What is the correct restructuring?
options: Split `CLAUDE.md` into three files and have engineers set an environment variable selecting which one loads.
Keep the sections in `CLAUDE.md` and add a preamble telling the model to ignore sections that do not apply to the current file.
Move all three into a single skill that the engineer invokes at the start of a session working on that file type.
Move each set of conventions into `.claude/rules/` with a glob matching its file type, so each loads only when a matching file is being edited.

whyRight.text: Root CLAUDE.md loads for every session regardless of what is being edited, which is why Terraform conventions are being paid for during React work. Path-scoped rules load only when a matching file is read, so each set of conventions costs nothing when it does not apply while still applying automatically when it does.

whyWrong.text: This builds a manual selection mechanism to replace one that already selects automatically by file path, and it fails as soon as a session touches two file types.
An instruction to ignore content does not stop it being sent. The tokens are spent when the request is assembled, so this adds a line to the cost rather than removing it.

Conventions that must shape every edit should not depend on someone remembering to invoke them. A skill is the on-demand mechanism, and this content needs to be resident whenever a matching file is touched.

questions.stem: The reviewer emits findings in four categories. Three are accurate; the performance category is wrong roughly 70% of the time. Developers have begun dismissing all four without reading them, and correctness findings are now being missed in review. What is the correct move while the performance prompt is being improved?
options: Keep all four active and reduce the performance category's volume by surfacing only its highest-severity findings.
Keep all four active and label performance findings as low-confidence, so developers can weigh them appropriately.
Turn the performance category off until its prompt is fixed, so the three reliable categories are read again.
Keep all four active and add a note asking developers to read the correctness findings even if they skip the others.

whyRight.text: A high false-positive rate in one category destroys trust in the whole output, which is what the dismissal pattern shows — the cost is now being paid in missed correctness findings, not in wasted time on performance ones. Disabling the unreliable category while its prompt is improved restores the credibility of the rest immediately.

whyWrong.text: Severity filtering reduces the count of wrong findings without raising their accuracy, so a smaller stream of mostly-wrong performance findings keeps the credibility problem alive at lower volume.

A label asks developers to do the filtering the system should have done, and they have already demonstrated they will not — they are dismissing everything rather than sorting it. The noise stays in the output either way.
This asks developers to sustain a distinction the tool is failing to make. Trust is being lost because the output as a whole is unreliable, and a note does not change what the output contains.

questions.stem: The team must migrate the pipeline off a deprecated test runner. The replacement is chosen and its basic invocation is documented, but the configuration mapping is unclear in three places, two custom reporters may have no equivalent at all, and roughly 40 spec files will need changing. How should Claude Code be used for this work?
options: Plan mode to work out the configuration mapping and the reporter question, then direct execution to carry out the agreed migration.
Plan mode throughout, including the edits, so each of the 40 files is reviewed before it is written.
Direct execution from the start, since the replacement runner is already chosen and the work is mechanical.
Direct execution on the configuration first, switching to plan mode if the reporters turn out to have no equivalent.

whyRight.text: This splits cleanly into an open part and a mechanical part. The mapping and the reporters are genuine unknowns that are expensive to get wrong across 40 files, so they are settled in plan mode first. Once the approach is agreed the edits are repetitive application, which is what direct execution is for. Plan the strategy, then execute it.

whyWrong.text: Extending planning across 40 mechanical edits adds review overhead to changes whose shape is no longer in question. Planning is for deciding the approach, not for gating its application.
Choosing the runner is not the same as knowing the migration. The configuration mapping is unclear and three reporters may need replacing, so the work is not mechanical yet.
The reporter uncertainty is stated in the requirements, not discovered mid-flight. Waiting for it to become a problem means finding out after configuration work already depends on an answer.

questions.stem: The nightly job runs four analyses across the repository. On one run the dependency-graph analysis fails on a malformed lockfile, after the complexity, coverage and dead-code analyses have all completed and produced their sections. The orchestrator's current handler aborts the run and writes nothing at all. What should it do instead?
options: Retry the whole run from the start, so the report is either complete or absent rather than partial.
Write the three completed analyses with an explicit note that the dependency-graph analysis failed and why, then decide whether that one is worth retrying on its own.
Write the three completed analyses and omit any mention of the fourth, so the report reads cleanly.
Write all four sections, marking the dependency-graph section as empty so the report's structure stays consistent.

whyRight.text: A failure in one branch should not discard three that succeeded. The orchestrator assesses the failure and chooses targeted recovery — publish what completed, record what did not and why, and retry only the failed analysis. That keeps the successful work and keeps the report honest about its own coverage.

whyWrong.text: Re-running everything throws away three completed analyses to retry one, and a lockfile that is malformed will still be malformed on the second attempt, so the run may produce nothing at all.
A report that omits the failure presents three-quarters coverage as the whole picture. A reader has no way to know the dependency graph was never examined.

An empty section reads as an analysis that ran and found nothing, which is a different and more damaging claim than an analysis that failed. Structural consistency is not worth a false statement about coverage.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to move three Claude workloads to the Message Batches API to cut cost: an interactive query tool a developer waits on, a pre-merge check that blocks the pipeline, and a monthly architecture report nobody reads until the following week. Select TWO properties of that API that constrain which of them can move.
options: There is no latency guarantee, and a batch may take up to 24 hours to complete.
A batch request cannot execute tools and continue reasoning from their results within the same request.
Batch requests are limited to a smaller context window than synchronous requests.
Batch results are returned unordered and without any identifier linking them to their inputs.

whyRight.text: Two properties rule workloads out. The absence of a latency SLA means nothing blocking can use it — results often arrive quickly and the design has to survive the 24-hour case. And a batch request cannot run a multi-turn tool-calling loop within itself, so any workload that needs to call a tool and reason from the result mid-processing must stay synchronous.

whyWrong.text: Batch requests are not given a smaller context window. Inventing a capacity limit would rule out large-document workloads that are in fact among the best candidates for batching.

Each request carries a caller-supplied identifier that is returned with its result, which is exactly what makes reassembly possible. Maintaining that join key is a discipline the corpus requires, not a limitation of the API.

questions.stem: The reviewer attaches a confidence score to each finding, and the pipeline auto-resolves anything above 0.9 without human review. A sample audit finds that 0.9-confidence findings about naming are right 96% of the time, while 0.9-confidence findings about concurrency are right 71% of the time. What does the pipeline need before it can keep auto-resolving?
options: Removal of the concurrency category from auto-resolution, leaving the uniform 0.9 threshold in place for the rest.
A single higher threshold of 0.95 applied uniformly, since the weaker type sets the safe operating point.
Calibration of the thresholds against a labelled set per finding type, so a cut-off reflects the accuracy that score actually predicts for that type.
A second confidence score from a separate prompt, auto-resolving only when both exceed 0.9.

whyRight.text: Raw confidence is not calibrated, and the audit shows the same 0.9 meaning two quite different things. Calibrating per finding type against labelled data turns the score into something whose threshold can be reasoned about — which is the prerequisite the corpus sets before confidence is allowed to drive an automated decision.

whyWrong.text: Excluding concurrency handles the one type the audit happened to examine and leaves every other type on an uncalibrated threshold. The next type with a similar gap is discovered the same way.
A uniform threshold set by the weakest type sends large volumes of accurate naming findings to human review, paying reviewer capacity to compensate for a scale mismatch rather than measuring it.
Two uncalibrated scores from the same model correlate, so agreement is weak evidence. It doubles the cost without establishing what either number predicts.

questions.stem: The reviewer's summary block is specified in four paragraphs of prose describing what each section should contain and how findings should be ordered. Across runs the sections appear in different orders and the ordering rule is applied inconsistently. An engineer proposes rewriting the four paragraphs more precisely. What should be done instead?
options: Rewrite the paragraphs with numbered rules and defined terms, removing the ambiguity from the prose.
Provide two or three worked examples pairing a set of findings with the exact summary block they should produce.
Add a validation step that reorders the sections after generation, so the prose no longer has to be precise.
Reduce the summary to a single section, so no ordering rule is needed.

whyRight.text: Four paragraphs of description have already been written and are still being read differently run to run. Concrete input-and-output examples remove the interpretation step rather than trying to narrow it — the model is shown the target instead of being told about it. The corpus's rule is examples first once prose has failed, not more prose.

whyWrong.text: More precise prose is still prose, still interpreted. This is the fifth attempt at the intervention that has already failed four times.
Post-processing enforces section order and cannot fix inconsistent application of the ordering rule inside each section. It also builds a repair step to avoid specifying the requirement properly.
Collapsing the structure removes the requirement rather than meeting it, and the summary loses the organisation that made it usable in review.

questions.stem: A generation step writes database migration scripts and a review step checks them against the schema before they are applied. Both currently run as consecutive turns in one session. Across roughly ninety migrations the review has never rejected a script, and two migrations that reached production had to be rolled back. What change makes the review meaningful?
options: Instruct the review turn to assume the script is wrong until it has verified each statement against the schema.
Move the review to a stronger model while keeping it in the generation session.
Run the review turn twice in the same session and reject if either pass objects.
Run the review as a separate instance receiving the script and the schema but none of the generation conversation.

whyRight.text: A reviewer sharing the generation session has the reasoning that produced every line already in front of it, and that context makes rejection unlikely — it is evaluating an argument it just made. An independent instance sees the script and the schema and nothing else, so it judges the artefact rather than the intent behind it.

whyWrong.text: An adversarial instruction is issued into the same contaminated context. The model still has its own justification for each statement available and is being asked to argue against itself.
Capability is not the constraint; access to the generation rationale is. A stronger model in the same session inherits the same reasons to accept what was written.
Two passes in one session share the same context and tend to reach the same conclusion. Repetition raises confidence in a correlated judgement rather than producing an independent one.

questions.stem: The nightly job emits a coverage report through a tool call with a JSON schema. Every payload parses. Finance-side consumers report that `lines_covered` sometimes exceeds `lines_total`, and that the reported percentage does not always match the two counts. What is needed?
options: A tighter schema constraining all three fields to non-negative numbers with the percentage bounded between 0 and 100.
Validation logic expressing the cross-field rules — covered never exceeds total, and the percentage is derived from the two — with the specific violation fed back for correction.
An instruction in the prompt reminding the model that covered lines cannot exceed total lines.
A schema requiring all three fields, so none can be omitted and left to be inferred downstream.

whyRight.text: These are semantic errors: every value is well-formed and correctly typed, and the relationships between them are wrong. A schema describes fields individually and cannot say that one must not exceed another or that a third is derived from both. Validation code expresses those rules, and its specific error message is what a retry can act on.

whyWrong.text: Range constraints on each field independently are all satisfied by the bad payloads — 900 covered of 800 total is two non-negative numbers, and a percentage between 0 and 100 can still disagree with them.
A prompt reminder makes the model's own arithmetic the control, which is what is failing. Nothing checks the output, so a bad payload still reaches the consumer.
All three fields are already present; none is being omitted. Requiredness governs presence and has no bearing on whether present values are consistent with each other.

questions.stem: The nightly job always performs the same three steps against the artefact store: fetch the manifest, verify its checksum, then record the result. The agent sometimes records without verifying, and sometimes verifies a manifest it fetched two steps earlier. An engineer proposes bundling all three into one `process_artefact` tool. When is that the right call?
options: When the three steps are always performed together in that order and the model has no legitimate reason to run them separately, bundling removes a sequencing decision it keeps getting wrong.
Never — bundling hides the individual steps from the model, so a failure in any one of them becomes harder to diagnose.
Only if the three steps are also exposed individually, so the model can choose the composite or the parts as it sees fit.
Only after a `PostToolUse` hook has been added to verify that the three steps ran in the right order.

whyRight.text: A composite tool is right when the steps are invariably performed together and the ordering is not a decision worth leaving to the model. Here that holds: three fixed steps, one order, no case for running them apart. Bundling them makes the sequence a property of the tool rather than something the model has to get right on every run.

whyWrong.text: Diagnosability is a real consideration and is handled by the composite returning structured per-step results. Ruling bundling out entirely discards the mechanism the corpus recommends for exactly this pattern.
Exposing both leaves the sequencing decision available, which is the decision being got wrong. It also widens the tool set, which works against selection reliability.
A PostToolUse hook observes ordering after the fact and cannot prevent a record written without a verification. It detects the failure the composite tool makes impossible.

questions.stem: The project `CLAUDE.md` has become hard to maintain: universal standards, the commit convention and the review checklist all sit in one file that several people edit. The team wants them in separate files while still loading together for every session. What supports this?
options: An `@path` import in `CLAUDE.md` referencing each of the separate files, so they are pulled in as part of the same load.
Placing the separate files alongside `CLAUDE.md` in `.claude/`, where every file in the directory is loaded automatically.
A `.claude/rules/` file per topic with a glob matching every path, which reproduces always-on loading.
A skill per topic with `disable-model-invocation` set, so each is loaded at session start rather than on request.

whyRight.text: `@path` imports are the supported way to modularise CLAUDE.md. The entry file references the others and they are pulled in as part of the same load, so the content still arrives in every session while each topic lives in its own file with its own edit history.

whyWrong.text: Loading is not a matter of dropping files into the directory and hoping they are picked up. CLAUDE.md is the entry point, and other files reach the context because it references them.
A match-everything glob is a fragile way of writing what CLAUDE.md already does, and it repurposes the file-scoped mechanism to carry content that is not file-scoped at all.
Skills load as invoked workflows, and disabling model invocation makes a skill less available rather than resident. It does not turn one into always-on context.

questions.stem: The same prompt against the same commit gives different verdicts on different runs — one run flags a naming violation the next ignores, and the pipeline's pass/fail parse sometimes fails outright because the summary wording changed. The team wants the CI review reproducible. Select TWO changes that address this.
options: Invoke Claude Code from the repository root so the project configuration is in the loaded hierarchy on every run.
Request structured output and branch the pipeline on parsed fields rather than on the wording of the printed text.
Raise the runner timeout so slow runs are not cut short mid-review.
Pin the review to a single reviewer machine, so the environment is identical between runs.

whyRight.text: Two different sources of variation are in play. If the run is started outside the repository the project configuration never loads, so the conventions applied differ from a local run — invoking from the root fixes what the model is told. And branching on parsed structured fields rather than on rendered prose removes the pipeline's sensitivity to how a verdict happens to be phrased.

whyWrong.text: A longer timeout prevents truncation and does nothing about two completed runs disagreeing. It addresses a failure mode that is not the one described.
Pinning to one machine makes the environment uniform and leaves both real causes in place, while removing the pipeline's ability to run anywhere. It is a constraint, not a fix.

questions.stem: A summarisation step must return a JSON object, and roughly one call in twelve begins with a sentence of preamble before the object, which breaks the parser. Tool-based structured output is not available for this step. What is the most direct way to constrain the response?
options: Lower the temperature so the model produces its most likely response, which is the bare object.
Add a system-prompt line stating that the response must contain no text outside the JSON object.
Strip everything before the first opening brace in post-processing.
Prefill the start of the assistant's response with the opening brace, so the model continues from inside the object.

whyRight.text: Prefilling seeds the beginning of the assistant's response, so the model resumes from a point that is already inside the JSON object and the preamble has nowhere to go. It constrains the shape at generation time rather than instructing towards it, which is what makes it the direct answer when a tool-call schema is not available.

whyWrong.text: Lower temperature narrows sampling around the model's existing tendencies, one of which is occasionally to introduce its answer. It makes the behaviour more consistent without deciding which behaviour.

An instruction of this kind is presumably already implied and is being followed eleven times in twelve. Restating it moves the rate rather than removing the failure, which prefilling does structurally.
Stripping before the first brace repairs the output after the fact and breaks whenever a preamble happens to contain a brace. It is the compensating cleanup rather than the constraint.

questions.stem: Each CI review is currently invoked with `--resume` against a long-lived session, so the reviewer 'remembers the repository'. The reviews have begun citing helper functions that were deleted a fortnight ago and referring to a directory layout that changed in the same window. What should the pipeline do?
options: Fork the long-lived session per run, so each review branches from the shared baseline without writing back to it.
Keep resuming and add an instruction telling the reviewer to re-read files before citing them.
Start each run in a fresh session and inject a short structured summary of any standing context the review needs.
Keep resuming and compact the long-lived session weekly to keep it from growing unbounded.

whyRight.text: A long-lived resumed session accumulates tool results describing a repository that keeps changing, and the agent reasons over them as though they were current — which is exactly the symptom. When prior results are broadly stale the corpus's answer is a fresh session with a structured summary injected: the conclusions carry forward, the outdated evidence does not.

whyWrong.text: A fork inherits everything up to the branch point, so each run starts from the same accumulated stale results. It isolates the runs from each other without removing what is making them wrong.

The stale results remain in history and remain available to reason from, so an instruction to re-read competes with content the model already has. Resume-and-inform is the right pattern when a small, nameable set of files changed, which is not this case.
Compaction bounds the size of the session and summarises stale content rather than discarding it, so outdated conclusions survive in condensed form. Growth is not the problem being described.

questions.stem: The nightly job summarises each of 30 modules in a loop. Some summaries end mid-sentence, and the loop treats them as complete and moves on. Inspecting the responses, the truncated ones carry `stop_reason` of `max_tokens`. How should the loop handle this?
options: Treat any value other than `end_turn` as unfinished and branch on which one it is — for `max_tokens`, continue the response or reduce what was requested, rather than accepting it as complete.
Treat `max_tokens` as equivalent to `end_turn`, since the model stopped producing output either way, and flag the summary for human review.
Set a higher output limit and treat any response that still truncates as a module too large to summarise.
Check whether the last character is a full stop and re-request the summary when it is not.

whyRight.text: `stop_reason` states why generation ended, and `max_tokens` means the response ran into the output limit rather than finishing. A loop that branches only on `tool_use` versus everything-else-is-done accepts truncated work as complete. The safe rule is that only `end_turn` means finished; every other value is a reason to look at what happened and act on it.

whyWrong.text: This preserves the conflation that caused the bug and adds a human to catch it afterwards. The API already distinguishes the two cases, so a review queue is being built to recover a signal that is being discarded.

Raising the limit reduces how often truncation occurs and leaves the loop unable to recognise it when it does. The second half declares a module unsummarisable on the basis of a limit rather than of its content.

Inspecting the text for a terminal full stop is natural-language parsing standing in for a deterministic field. A summary can end mid-sentence after a full stop in an abbreviation, and a complete one can end without one.

questions.stem: One prompt currently asks the model to identify each document in the bundle, extract the fields belonging to each, reconcile the repair quotes against the adjuster's narrative, and produce a settlement recommendation. Output quality is poor and the failures are hard to attribute to any one part. What is the correct restructuring?
options: Keep the single prompt and require the model to work through the four tasks in order, showing its intermediate results.
